theme: Solomon established on the throne; David’s final charge
readingInstruction: Read 1 Kings 1:1-2:46. David is old, and the question of who will succeed him comes to a head. Read David’s charge to Solomon in chapter 2 with care.
settingTheScene: The first book of Kings opens with an elderly, cold David and a succession crisis. His son Adonijah declares himself king, but Nathan and Bathsheba persuade David to keep his promise that Solomon will reign. Solomon is anointed at Gihon. Before he dies, David gives Solomon a final charge. Then Solomon deals with those who threaten his throne.
observation: Adonijah, “a very handsome man,” says, “I will be king” (1:5-6).
Nathan and Bathsheba remind David of his oath that Solomon would reign (1:11-31).
Zadok the priest anoints Solomon with oil from the tent, and the people shout, “Long live King Solomon!” (1:38-40).
David’s charge: “Be strong, and show yourself a man, and keep the charge of the LORD your God, walking in his ways” (2:2-3).
“That the LORD may establish his word that he spoke concerning me, saying, If your sons pay close attention to their way… you shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel” (2:4).
David dies: “Then David slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David” (2:10).
Solomon has Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei dealt with (2:13-46).
“So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon” (2:46).
interpretation:
The first chapters of Kings show the covenant of 2 Samuel 7 being worked out in real life. Adonijah’s bid for the throne follows the pattern of Absalom: a handsome prince, an entourage, and a claim made while the father is weak. But God has chosen Solomon, and God’s choice stands. Nathan, who spoke the covenant, and Bathsheba, who knows the promise, ensure that David’s oath is honored. The promise of God is kept through the quiet work of faithful people.

David’s last words to Solomon are the passage to read most carefully. They are a charge: “Keep the charge of the LORD your God, walking in his ways, and keeping his statutes… that you may prosper in all that you do.” The promise of the dynasty is tied to the obedience of the king. This is the pattern of the Davidic covenant as it unfolds: the promise of God is certain, but the individual kings who enjoy it must walk in faithfulness. It sets up the question the rest of Kings will answer: will the sons of David obey?

David also leaves Solomon some hard instructions about Joab and Shimei. These can read as vengeful, but David is passing on matters of justice that he had left unresolved. Joab had murdered Abner and Amasa. Shimei had cursed the king. Solomon, in his early reign, removes these threats. The narrative presents it as the establishment of the kingdom.

Notice the quiet line: “David slept with his fathers.” The man who was a shepherd, a fugitive, a king, an adulterer, a poet, and a penitent dies in peace. His reign lasted forty years. The kingdom now passes to his son.

The last line of the chapter is a hinge: “So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.” It is a statement of fulfillment, and also a question about what will happen next.
connection: Jesus is the true Son of David who was anointed at the Jordan and cried, “It is finished.” Unlike Solomon, he needed no one to clear away his rivals. He conquered death by his own death. The charge to “be strong and keep the charge of the LORD” was kept perfectly only by him (Hebrews 3:6). Luke 22:29: “I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom.”
application:
If you are a parent or mentor, think about what charge you would leave to those who come after you.

Ask where you need to keep your word, as David did.

Thank God that the promised kingdom is established by Christ and not dependent on human obedience.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for keeping his promises through quiet and faithful people.
Ask him to help you walk in his ways.
Thank him for the true Son of David.
